chunks: How an MCU talks to peripherals. The question: How does a microcontroller interact with external peripherals?
A microcontroller doesn't wiggle its pins one by one from software. Each hardware block on the chip, called a peripheral, has a set of control registers at fixed addresses.
Firmware (the chip's program) writes settings into those registers, tells the block to go, and reads status back. The block then drives the pins with the right timing.
Which block you use depends on what is attached.
Picture a control panel on a machine in the next room. You flip switches to choose the settings, press "go", and read the indicator lights to see progress.
To know when the job is done, you can stare at the light (polling), wait for a bell (an interrupt), or hand the job to an assistant who carries the results to your desk (DMA).
The registers are the panel, and the peripheral is the machine.
Left: a pushbutton with a pull-up resistor gives a defined high when open and low when pressed (an input, ideally debounced).
Top right: an LED with a series resistor on an output pin. Bottom right: an I2C sensor on SDA and SCL, each pulled up to VDD because the bus is open-drain.
Each of the three uses a different MCU mechanism: GPIO input, GPIO output, serial peripheral.
Register: a control slot at a fixed address. Writing to it sets up a peripheral or sends data.
GPIO pin: a general-purpose pin the firmware can drive high or low, or read as an input.
Serial bus: a few wires that send bits one after another, such as I2C, SPI and UART ("I2C, SPI and UART: how each works").
Polling: the processor repeatedly checks a status flag until the job is done. Interrupt: the peripheral signals the processor when it needs attention.
DMA: a helper block that moves data to and from memory without the processor.
To light an LED (a light-emitting diode), firmware makes three register writes: switch on the clock for the pin's group, set the pin as an output, then write a 1.
The LED uses up about 2. 0 volts and should get 5 milliamps, so from 3. 3 volts it needs a resistor of (3. 3-2. 0) over 5 milliamps equals 260 ohms.
A standard 270 ohms gives about 4. 8 milliamps. That is the whole idea.
"The firmware talks to hardware through memory-mapped registers: configure a peripheral, then read and write its data and status registers.
Depending on the device, the pins are GPIO for on/off signals, ADC for analog in, timers and PWM for waveforms, or a serial bus like I2C, SPI, UART or CAN for smart peripherals.
Data moves by polling, interrupts or DMA, depending on rate and latency.
And electrically I make sure the levels match, open-drain buses have pull-ups, and pins are protected and current-limited."
